questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a gene, an allele and a genotype?
options: A gene is one version of a trait; an allele is its locus; a genotype is the visible trait
A gene is a whole chromosome; alleles are the genes on it; a genotype is all of a person's DNA
A gene is a pair of alleles; an allele is one chromosome; a genotype is the person's phenotype
A gene codes for a trait; alleles are its versions; a genotype is the alleles a person has
questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA coding for a product, alleles are alternative forms of that gene, and the genotype is the combination of alleles an individual carries. The visible trait is the phenotype, not the genotype.

questions.stem: A pea plant has the genotype Tt for stem height. Which term describes this genotype?
options: Homozygous recessive
Hemizygous
Heterozygous
Homozygous dominant
questions.explanation: Tt has two different alleles of the gene, so it is heterozygous. Hemizygous describes having only one copy of a gene, as males do for X-linked genes.

questions.stem: A man has blood group O. What is his genotype for the ABO gene?
options: IA IB
IA i
IB i
ii
questions.explanation: The i allele is recessive to both IA and IB, so group O appears only when a person has two i alleles. IA i gives group A and IB i gives group B.

questions.stem: What does Mendel's law of segregation (random segregation) state?
options: The two alleles of a gene separate, so each gamete receives only one of them
Alleles of different genes always stay together in the same gamete
Each gamete receives both alleles of every gene the parent carries
Dominant alleles pass into gametes more often than recessive alleles
questions.explanation: In meiosis the homologous chromosomes carrying the two alleles separate, so each gamete gets one allele of each gene, with equal chance of either. Gametes are haploid, so they cannot carry both alleles of a gene.

questions.stem: In humans (2n = 46), how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment alone produce from one person?
options: 46, one per chromosome
2^23, about 8.4 million
23^2, which is 529
2^46, about 70 trillion
questions.explanation: Each of the 23 homologous pairs lines up independently, giving 2 choices per pair, so 2^23 = 8,388,608 combinations. About 70 trillion is roughly the number of combinations of one sperm and one egg after random fertilisation.

questions.stem: Why does random fertilisation add to the variation produced by meiosis?
options: Any one of a huge number of different sperm can fuse with any of many different eggs
Fertilisation causes crossing over between maternal and paternal chromosomes
The zygote receives two full sets of chromosomes from each of its two parents
Fusion of the gametes creates new alleles by mixing the two sets of DNA together
questions.explanation: Each parent can make millions of genetically different gametes, and which sperm meets which egg is a matter of chance, so the number of possible zygotes is enormous. Crossing over happens during meiosis, before fertilisation, and the zygote gets one set from each parent.

questions.stem: During prophase I, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments. What is the result?
options: New combinations of alleles on the chromatids
New alleles made by changes to the base sequence
Gametes with extra copies of some chromosomes
Identical sister chromatids in every gamete
questions.explanation: Crossing over swaps sections between maternal and paternal chromatids, so alleles that were on different homologues end up on the same chromatid. It recombines existing alleles; new alleles arise only by mutation.

questions.stem: An organism has two pairs of homologous chromosomes, labelled A and a, and B and b. Without crossing over, which set of gametes can meiosis produce?
options: AA, aa, BB and bb
Aa, Bb, Aa and Bb
AaBb in every gamete
AB, Ab, aB and ab
questions.explanation: Each gamete receives one chromosome from each homologous pair, and the pairs assort independently, giving four combinations. Gametes never receive both members of a pair, so Aa or AaBb gametes are impossible.

questions.stem: Which event in meiosis is the basis of independent assortment?
options: Random orientation of homologous pairs at the equator in metaphase I
Separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles in anaphase II
Replication of every chromosome before meiosis begins
Formation of four haploid cells at the end of telophase II
questions.explanation: Each homologous pair lines up independently of the others in metaphase I, so the maternal and paternal chromosomes of different pairs are sorted into gametes in random combinations. Separation of sister chromatids happens later and does not produce this effect.

questions.stem: Huntington's disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. What does this mean?
options: Two copies of the allele on an autosome are needed for the disease to appear
The allele is carried on the X chromosome, so it mainly affects males
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, so only fathers can pass it on
One copy of the allele on a non-sex chromosome is enough to cause the disease
questions.explanation: Autosomal means the gene is on one of the 22 pairs of non-sex chromosomes, and dominant means a single copy is expressed. Needing two copies would make the condition recessive.

questions.stem: Which condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern?
options: Red-green colour blindness
Cystic fibrosis
Huntington's disease
Haemophilia A
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis appears only in people with two copies of the faulty allele of an autosomal gene. Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant, and haemophilia A and red-green colour blindness are X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: Two parents are both carriers (Ff) of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition. What is the probability that a child of theirs will have cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Ff x Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff and ff in equal proportions, so 1 in 4 children is expected to be ff and affected. 3/4 is the probability of being unaffected.

questions.stem: Two carriers (Ff) of cystic fibrosis have a child who does not have the condition. What is the probability that this child is a carrier?
questions.explanation: The child is not ff, so only FF, Ff and Ff remain possible, and two of these three are carriers. The answer 1/2 is the carrier probability before the child's phenotype is known.

questions.stem: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant. A heterozygous man and an unaffected woman have children. What proportion of their children are expected to be affected?
questions.explanation: Hh x hh gives Hh and hh in equal numbers, so half the children are expected to inherit the dominant allele and be affected.

questions.stem: Which allele relationship gives a heterozygote with a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes?
options: Complete dominance
Sex linkage
Incomplete dominance
Codominance
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully expressed, so the heterozygote is a blend, such as pink flowers from red and white. In codominance both phenotypes appear side by side.

questions.stem: In four o'clock plants, red-flowered plants (RR) crossed with white-flowered plants (WW) give pink offspring. A pink plant is crossed with a white plant. What phenotype ratio is expected?
options: 3 pink : 1 white
All pink
1 pink : 1 white
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
questions.explanation: RW x WW gives RW (pink) and WW (white) in equal numbers. The 1 : 2 : 1 ratio comes from crossing two pink plants.

questions.stem: Which observation shows codominance rather than incomplete dominance?
options: A grey mouse is born to a black and a white parent
A pale blue flower grows from dark blue and white parents
A roan calf has both red hairs and white hairs in its coat
A pink snapdragon grows from red and white parent plants
questions.explanation: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed side by side, so each red hair and white hair is visible. Pink, grey and pale blue are blends, which is incomplete dominance.

questions.stem: In cattle, red (CR CR) and white (CW CW) coats are codominant, and the heterozygote is roan. Two roan cattle are mated. What proportion of their calves are expected to be roan?
questions.explanation: CR CW x CR CW gives CR CR, CR CW, CR CW and CW CW, so 2 of 4, or half, are roan. A quarter are red and a quarter white, so 3/4 would wrongly treat roan as dominant.

questions.stem: Which statement describes multiple allele inheritance?
options: A gene has three or more alleles in the population, but each person has two
A trait is controlled by many genes, each with only two alleles
Each person carries three or more alleles of the same gene
A gene has two alleles that are found on both the X and Y chromosomes
questions.explanation: A multiple allele gene, such as the ABO gene with IA, IB and i, has more than two alleles in the population, but a diploid person still carries only two. A trait controlled by many genes is polygenic, which is different.

questions.stem: Which genotypes give blood group A?
options: IA i only
IA IA only
IA IA or IA i
IA IB or IA i
questions.explanation: IA is dominant to i, so both IA IA and IA i give group A. IA IB gives group AB because IA and IB are codominant.

questions.stem: A woman with blood group AB has children with a man with blood group O. Which blood groups are possible in their children?
options: A, B, AB and O
A, B and AB only
A and B only
AB and O only
questions.explanation: IA IB x ii gives IA i, which is group A, and IB i, which is group B. No child can be AB, because the father gives only i, or O, because the mother always gives IA or IB.

questions.stem: A child has blood group O and the mother has blood group A. Which man's blood group would rule him out as the father?
options: AB
A
B
O
questions.explanation: A group O child is ii, so it must receive an i allele from each parent. A group AB man (IA IB) has no i allele to give, while men of group A or B may be heterozygous and a group O man is ii.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as red-green colour blindness more common in males?
options: Testosterone switches on the recessive allele in male cells only
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Males have two X chromosomes, so they are twice as likely to inherit it
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, which only males have
questions.explanation: Males are XY, so they have only one allele of an X-linked gene and a single recessive allele shows in the phenotype. Females need two copies, one on each X, to be affected.

questions.stem: A colour-blind man (Xb Y) and a woman homozygous for normal vision (XB XB) have children. Which outcome is expected?
options: Half of all the children are colour-blind, whatever their sex
All daughters are carriers and all sons have normal vision
Half the sons are colour-blind and half the daughters are carriers
All sons are colour-blind and all daughters are non-carriers
questions.explanation: Daughters receive the father's Xb and the mother's XB, so they are carriers; sons receive his Y and her XB, so they have normal vision. A father never passes his X chromosome to his sons.

questions.stem: A carrier woman (XB Xb) and a colour-blind man (Xb Y) have children. What proportion of their daughters are expected to be colour-blind?
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives Xb from her father and either XB or Xb from her mother, so half are Xb Xb and colour-blind. A quarter is the proportion of all children who are colour-blind daughters, not the proportion of daughters.

questions.stem: The crosses Aa x Aa (autosomal) and XA Xa x XA Y (X-linked) both give 1/4 of all offspring with the recessive phenotype. How do the results of the two crosses differ?
options: In the X-linked cross every affected offspring is a son, and half the sons are affected
In the X-linked cross every affected offspring is a daughter, and half the daughters are affected
In the X-linked cross a quarter of each sex is affected, exactly as in the autosomal cross
In the X-linked cross half the daughters and a quarter of the sons are affected
questions.explanation: Daughters all receive the father's XA, so none is affected, while sons receive XA or Xa from the mother, so half the sons are affected. In the autosomal cross a quarter of each sex is affected.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes X-linked inheritance from autosomal inheritance?
options: X-linked alleles are always dominant, while autosomal alleles can be recessive
X-linked genes come only from the father, while autosomal genes come from both
Males carry only one allele of the gene, so phenotype ratios differ between the sexes
X-linked genes have three or more alleles, while autosomal genes have only two
questions.explanation: Because males are hemizygous for X-linked genes, males and females show different ratios. Sons receive their X chromosome from their mother, not their father.

questions.stem: In cats, an X-linked gene has alleles for orange (XO) and black (XB) fur, and heterozygous females are tortoiseshell, with patches of both colours. Why are tortoiseshell cats almost always female?
options: Males inherit the colour gene only from their father, so have one colour
Two X chromosomes are needed to carry both alleles, and males have one
The orange allele is lethal in males, so only females survive with it
Tortoiseshell is a Y-linked trait, so males can never express it
questions.explanation: A cat must be heterozygous for this X-linked gene to show both colours, which requires two X chromosomes. Males normally have one X and so are either orange or black; males inherit their X from their mother.

questions.stem: A tortoiseshell female cat (XO XB) is mated with a black male (XB Y). What proportion of their female kittens are expected to be tortoiseshell?
questions.explanation: Every female kitten gets XB from her father and either XO or XB from her mother, so half are XO XB (tortoiseshell) and half XB XB (black). A quarter is the proportion of all kittens that are tortoiseshell.

questions.stem: In a pedigree chart, what does a horizontal line joining a square and a circle represent?
options: Two individuals with the same phenotype
Identical twins from one fertilised egg
A mating between the two individuals
Two siblings with the same parents
questions.explanation: A horizontal line between a male (square) and a female (circle) shows a mating, and a vertical line drops from it to their offspring. Siblings hang from a separate horizontal sibship line.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, a trait appears in every generation, every affected child has at least one affected parent, and males and females are affected equally. Which mode of inheritance is most likely?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
questions.explanation: A dominant allele is expressed whenever it is present, so the trait does not skip generations, and equal numbers of each sex suggest an autosome. Recessive traits often skip generations.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, a trait skips generations and affects far more males than females, and affected males usually have unaffected parents. Which mode of inheritance is most likely?
options: X-linked dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Skipped generations point to a recessive allele, and a strong excess of affected males points to the X chromosome, because males need only one copy. Autosomal recessive traits affect both sexes about equally.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, an affected woman and an unaffected man have an unaffected son. Which mode of inheritance does this rule out?
options: Autosomal dominant
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive
questions.explanation: An affected woman with an X-linked recessive trait is Xa Xa, so every son would receive Xa and be affected. A heterozygous mother with an X-linked dominant or autosomal trait could still have an unaffected son.

questions.stem: In a pedigree for an autosomal recessive condition, two unaffected parents have an affected son. What are the parents' genotypes?
options: Both are heterozygous carriers
Both are homozygous dominant
One is homozygous dominant and one homozygous recessive
One is heterozygous and one is homozygous recessive
questions.explanation: The son is aa, so he received an a allele from each parent, yet both parents are unaffected, so each must be Aa. An aa parent would show the condition.

questions.stem: Unaffected parents have an affected daughter with an autosomal recessive condition, and an unaffected son. The son has children with a woman who is homozygous dominant. What is the probability that a given grandchild is a carrier?
questions.explanation: The parents are both carriers, so the unaffected son has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, and a carrier father passes the allele to half his children: 2/3 x 1/2 = 1/3. The answer 2/3 is the son's own carrier probability.

questions.stem: Why do geneticists use pedigrees, rather than designed crosses, to study inheritance in humans?
options: Pedigrees reveal the DNA base sequence of each person
Humans cannot be crossed experimentally, and families are small
Punnett squares apply only to plants and not to animals
Human alleles do not follow the law of segregation
questions.explanation: Controlled breeding of humans is unethical and generations are long, so geneticists trace a trait through existing families. Human alleles segregate just like those of other organisms, and Punnett squares can be used to predict human offspring.

questions.stem: A cross of two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt) gives 290 tall and 110 short plants. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The result is close to the 1 : 1 ratio expected from this cross
The result is close to the expected 3 : 1 ratio, differing only by chance
The result shows that tall is incompletely dominant over short
The result shows that the gene for height is carried on a sex chromosome
questions.explanation: Of 400 plants, a 3 : 1 ratio predicts 300 tall and 100 short, so 290 and 110 is a close fit; fertilisation is random, so small differences are expected. Incomplete dominance would give a third, intermediate phenotype.
